titleStmt.title: Ghosts in the Machine: Feminist Digital Humanities and the Hidden Labor behind AI

dhq:bio.p: Amanda Furiasse (PhD, Florida State University) is Associate Professor of Digital Humanities and Medical Humanities at Nova Southeastern University. Her research interests converge around religion, technology, and medicine with a particular focus on AI applications in healthcare. She is senior producer of the Florida 2100: Tales of Tomorrow podcast and multimedia project, and host of the Applied Humanities podcast.

dhq:abstract.p: This review essay examines Feminist Digital Humanities: Intersections in Practice, edited by Lisa Marie Rhody and Susan Schreibman, arguing that the volume challenges the myth of the autonomous machine by foregrounding the collaborative labor that sustains digital scholarship. Through its focus on reading, infrastructure, and pedagogy, the collection demonstrates that digital knowledge emerges through routine practices of human care, maintenance, and interpretation that often disappear behind finished computational projects. Extending these insights to contemporary AI, the review argues that the appearance of machine autonomy is an ideological effect produced by obscuring the historically feminized labor on which digital knowledge and artificial intelligence continue to depend.

dhq:teaser.p: Book review of Feminist Digital Humanities: Intersections in Practice, edited by Lisa Marie Rhody and Susan Schreibman

div.head: Introduction
div.p: In 1804, Joseph-Marie Jacquard introduced a loom that used punched cards to control the lifting of warp threads, allowing complex textile patterns to be reproduced mechanically. Histories of computing often present the loom as a precursor to programming because its punched cards translated a design into a sequence of instructions that a machine could execute [Essinger 2004]. Yet this familiar origin story preserves only one part of the loom’s significance and obscures the skilled textile labor on which the system depended, particularly women’s expertise in pattern making, weaving, thread, tension, and material. As a result, Jacquard is largely celebrated as the inventor of a programmable machine, while the women’s expertise and labor that made that innovation possible have largely disappeared from historical memory.

It is precisely this relationship between technological innovation and historical erasure that Lisa Marie Rhody and Susan Schreibman explore in Feminist Digital Humanities: Intersections in Practice. Instead of asking only what DH preserves or produces, the collection asks whose labor, experience, and authority become hidden within the very systems that promise to make knowledge more transparent and accessible. In doing so, their edited volume demonstrates how DH as a field depends upon forms of collaboration that cut across disciplinary, technical, and institutional boundaries, making collaborative labor central to DH’s scholarly outputs.

div.head: “Bringing Theory into Practice”
div.p: The volume’s approach to feminism is distinctive in that Rhody and Schreibman define it through the everyday work of building archives, designing infrastructures, organizing collaborative research, teaching computational methods, and sustaining digital projects over time. As they observe, “Feminist DH practice has much to offer in terms of how we move forward as a field at large to meet the ever-growing challenges confronting the humanities in the twenty-first century, including how to represent and interpret the past, build for the future, and prepare future generations to continue our work” [Rhody and Schreibman 2025, 9]. Feminism, in this context, is not simply a theoretical framework brought to DH but a way of working with and organizing labor.

Importantly, that definition of feminism shifts attention away from what DH produces and toward the conditions under which digital knowledge is made. The central question is therefore not simply what DH studies, but how scholarship is organized. Who builds digital projects, maintains their infrastructure, teaches their methods, and ensures that they remain usable over time? Just as importantly, whose contributions are recognized as intellectual work, and whose continue to be categorized as technical assistance, administrative support, service, or care? Divided into three sections, the collection addresses those questions through three interrelated domains of practice. The first explores reading, asking how feminist methods reshape interpretation, recovery, and analysis. Here, reading becomes a form of scholarly work that determines not only what is seen and heard but also what can be known.

For example, Tanya Clement’s chapter, “Playback Is a Bitch,” demonstrates that reading itself is a form of scholarly practice whose labor often disappears once interpretation appears complete. Examining recordings of Anne Sexton’s poetry readings and therapy sessions, Clement argues that playback technologies do not simply recover an original voice but create the conditions under which interpretation becomes possible. Listening requires repeated acts of pausing, replaying, comparing, and isolating breaths, hesitations, changes in tone, and moments of silence that would otherwise pass unnoticed. These interpretive acts emerge through the combined work of the recording apparatus, the archive, and the listener, making the recording a “situated, sociotechnical phenomenon” rather than a transparent record of the past [Rhody and Schreibman 2025, 16]. The finished interpretation consequently obscures the practices that produced it, encouraging readers to mistake scholarly knowledge for the direct recovery of archival evidence instead of the cumulative labor through which that evidence becomes meaningful.

Developing this insight, the second collection of chapters shifts the focus to infrastructures and explores how platforms, archives, databases, laboratories, and collaborative networks are active sites where labor is organized, authority is distributed, and access is either enabled or constrained. In the case of the DH lab, Jacqueline Wernimont and Nikko L. Stevens’s chapter asks whether such spaces can support feminist DH if its structure continues to reproduce the hierarchies of the university, organizing digital work through a principal-investigator model in which faculty define the project, students and staff provide technical labor, and credit remains unevenly distributed. Wernimont and Stevens respond to this problem by developing a collaborative model for research, reimagining DH infrastructure as a shared workspace in which authority, expertise, and responsibility are distributed across participants rather than concentrated around a single project director.

Likewise, Nanna Bonde Thylstrup, Daniela Agostinho, Katrine Dirckinck-Holmfeld, and Kristin Veel demonstrate that repairing the archive requires more than recovering materials that have been excluded from the historical record. Their chapter argues that archival injustice is also produced through the classificatory practices that organize digital collections, including metadata standards, search interfaces, cataloging systems, and institutional protocols that determine how records are described, connected, and retrieved. Adding marginalized voices to a digital archive therefore does little if the infrastructures governing discovery and interpretation continue to privilege the same historical assumptions. Reparative practice requires rethinking the systems of classification through which archives produce historical knowledge in the first place.

The final section turns from the issue of archives and infrastructures to pedagogy itself, asking how feminist DH transforms the everyday practices through which computational knowledge is taught and reproduced in the classroom. Lisa Marie Rhody’s chapter, for instance, demonstrates how the practice of teaching code can itself become a feminist intervention. Using Jupyter notebooks, she encourages students to reflect on the assumptions embedded within computational methods while treating experimentation and critical reflection as integral to computational work. Students document their reasoning alongside their code, complete reflective writing assignments, and are evaluated on experimentation rather than technical mastery. Like the collection, Rhody’s pedagogy insists that DH should be evaluated not only by the tools it produces but by the forms of labor, reflection, and collaboration through which those tools come to acquire meaning over time.

div.head: The Invisible Hands of DH
div.p: Read together, these essays insist that digital projects never emerge fully formed. Archives depend upon cataloging and description, collaborative research depends upon maintenance and shared authorship, and computational methods depend upon teaching before they can become scholarly practice. Yet these activities rarely remain visible once a project is complete. What survives is the archive, the website, or the publication rather than the labor that produced it.

Donna Haraway’s [Haraway 2016] distinction between sympoiesis (“making-with”) and autopoiesis (“self-making”) provides a useful way to understand this insight. As in the case of Clement’s “Playback Is a Bitch,” the voice that seems to become newly available through digital access is not simply “found” in the archive. It becomes audible only through the combined work of Sexton’s recorded voice, the material condition of the original tape, digitization technologies, playback software, and the scholar who repeatedly pauses, replays, isolates, compares, and interprets breaths, hesitations, and changes in tone. Meaning therefore does not reside within the recording itself but only emerges through the interpretive labor that digital playback makes possible, even as that labor disappears behind the finished scholarly product.

Thylstrup, Agostinho, Dirckinck-Holmfeld, and Veel extend that insight from listening to archival organization itself. If playback technologies make interpretation possible, metadata standards, cataloging practices, search interfaces, and institutional protocols organize the conditions under which those records become audible and visible. Yet because these classificatory practices are embedded within the archive itself, they often disappear, creating the impression that digital collections simply reveal historical evidence rather than actively producing the pathways through which that evidence is encountered. The archive thus appears to function autonomously precisely because the labor of organizing, describing, and maintaining it recedes from view once the system is in place.

Offering a global perspective on this issue, Dhanashree Thorat’s chapter on teaching in Pune, India effectively reveals how computation could not function without teachers and students engaging in continual acts of translation, explanation, troubleshooting, and revision. Once students complete a text analysis or mapping project, however, this pedagogical work is largely obscured. Computational expertise consequently comes to appear as an individual accomplishment or even property of the software itself, obscuring the instructional and collaborative labor that made those tools usable in the first place.

div.head: The Myth of the Autonomous Machine
div.p: Although the volume offers an important corrective to claims about the autonomy of digital technologies, it stops just short of asking what happens when the collaborative practices it so carefully recovers come to appear as machine intelligence itself. Like the digital archive before it, artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning systems do not simply “find” answers, “read” documents, or “recognize” patterns. Their outputs depend upon accumulated acts of writing, annotation, classification, programming, maintenance, and interpretation that become compressed into the appearance of an immediate computational response. What appears as autonomous intelligence is therefore less a technical achievement than an ideological effect that is only produced by actively and deliberately concealing the human labor and institutional infrastructures through which that knowledge is made.

Once autonomy is understood as an effect of concealment rather than a property of the machine itself, the question is no longer whether AI will replace human labor, but how human labor is rendered invisible in the first place. Mary L. Gray and Siddharth Suri [Gray and Suri 2019] identify this hidden labor as “ghost work,” the dispersed human effort that allows automated systems to appear seamless, efficient, and self-sufficient. In the context of feminist DH, ghost work reveals that the fantasy of autonomous computation depends on the systematic disappearance of the labor that sustains it. It also extends one of the volume’s central insights by showing that the work most readily concealed by digital systems has historically been the kinds of care, maintenance, annotation, and support labor disproportionately performed by women.

AI and machine learning systems can appear to replace human expertise only when the labor that sustains them is reclassified as routine, technical, or merely supportive. As David Grier argues, such logic has deep historical roots in the development of computing itself [Grier 2005]. Throughout the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries, women were employed as “computers” not because their work lacked intellectual complexity, but because institutions framed their calculations as mechanical assistance rather than scientific reasoning. By defining computation as repetitive service instead of original inquiry, the knowledge embedded in their labor became increasingly invisible, allowing later computational technologies to appear autonomous rather than as products of accumulated human expertise.

This longer history of women’s computational labor clarifies the stakes of Rhody and Schreibman’s volume as well as its value for scholars of DH and readers working in feminist science and technology studies, media studies, library and information science, and AI studies. The danger is not simply that women’s work disappears from the history of science and technology, but that this disappearance becomes the very mechanism by which technological progress is measured. By foregrounding the human labor that underwrites digital knowledge, Feminist Digital Humanities ultimately challenges the assumption that technological progress is measured by the disappearance of human effort.

At a moment when AI is increasingly described as replacing human expertise, the volume offers a timely reminder that digital systems have always depended upon human labor whose visibility has itself become a political question. Rather than asking what machines can do without people, the collection instead demonstrates that the appearance of machine autonomy is itself produced through the historical erasure of labor that makes computation possible. Like the Jacquard loom before it, the future of DH will ultimately depend on its willingness to make visible the forms of labor, care, and collaboration that history so often renders invisible.
